lxc_1f5adc0e3c553a99.text: Spicy curry has a long journey.

lxc_b67d6bd07f1c4276.text: See how it traveled through cultures, meet the spice team, and discover how it changed in Japan.

lxc_d8585a2a571b6ce9.text: When people in Japan hear "curry," they may picture a thick brown sauce with rice, potatoes, carrots, onions, and meat.

lxc_df708fab52142111.text: However, curry is not one recipe.

lxc_0b667d30b214bdc7.text: Across South Asia and other parts of the world, cooks make many different dishes with spices.

lxc_abc4649345bc29da.text: Some are dry, some have a lot of sauce, and some use coconut milk or tomatoes.

lxc_bed8c37e5f229046.text: Many of these dishes also have their own local names.

lxc_137a92dd9bf0c8d0.text: The wide English word "curry" became common through British colonial contact with South Asia.

lxc_7820336bb09ff2c4.text: It is useful as a big food category, but it cannot show every local tradition.

lxc_f369f9479d444bfc.text: There is no single spice mix for every curry.

lxc_50f189b453561c7c.text: One curry powder may contain turmeric, coriander, cumin, chili pepper, fenugreek, cinnamon, cardamom, black pepper, and more.

lxc_45275ff1bfc2ea7d.text: Think of the spices as a team.

lxc_171f2fdc6b8389d6.text: Turmeric often brings yellow color and an earthy note.

lxc_72ae5389cd7f1420.text: Cumin gives a warm, rich smell.

lxc_a0c5e455c6851ac1.text: Coriander seed can add a lighter, slightly citrus-like taste.

lxc_631a5a49c0e1b882.text: Chili pepper brings the burning feeling we call heat.

lxc_b5dafa80c057aa07.text: Cinnamon and cardamom can add a sweet aroma.

lxc_7f795c8e871a59ea.text: A cook changes the amount of each spice to build a different result.

lxc_5a9dacfe6c03ae90.text: That is why two curries can smell and taste very different.

lxc_21f2f2793ec22422.text: Here is a useful curry test: notice heat, aroma, and depth.

lxc_116cb61e20d5064d.text: Heat is the burning feeling from chili.

lxc_a37f6749a09a3c2a.text: Researchers explain that capsaicin, a substance in chili peppers, activates nerves that also respond to heat.

lxc_afd4ac04270e4d72.text: Your curry can therefore feel hot even when its temperature is not very high.

lxc_b73ccc2b3757c146.text: Aroma is what reaches your nose, such as warm cumin or sweet cardamom.

lxc_3cb168c0c15bccfb.text: Depth means the flavor feels full rather than simple.

lxc_9db42bee38ebdbe0.text: Onions, garlic, ginger, toasted spices, broth, fat, and cooking time can all add depth.

lxc_f582fce0e1148c2b.text: A curry can be mild but still have a strong aroma and deep flavor.

lxc_9a32c7f4f7b0afbd.text: Japanese curry has a travel story with several stops.

lxc_29350346a226fdb8.text: Its deeper roots are in South Asian spice traditions.

lxc_f4a38ce9e0db8166.text: Under British colonial rule, British cooks and companies turned the idea into commercial curry powder.

lxc_f5f9e3f9cf8ddf8d.text: The powder made a complex mix of spices easier to buy and move.

lxc_c4426206a40c88b8.text: This British-style product then entered Japan in the Meiji period, when many Western foods were becoming known there.

lxc_58a53ee278fd9c71.text: Japanese cooks did not simply copy one Indian dish.

lxc_242c8d1270e18da2.text: They received a British version and changed it again for local ingredients, rice, and everyday meals.

lxc_603e2a29e2de7909.text: Imagine a curry passport with three stamps: South Asia, Britain, and Japan.

lxc_4748c15b3ab8ee77.text: In Japan, curry became a thick sauce served over rice.

lxc_2db03923150a91cd.text: Carrots, potatoes, onions, and meat became common ingredients.

lxc_86337d52276264e8.text: One well-known story connects this style with the Japanese Navy.

lxc_29f190accc1d3600.text: Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries presents it as one theory, not the only story.

lxc_453cdce794291c07.text: British naval curry was thickened, paired with rice, and used as a practical meal with meat and vegetables.

lxc_d4010e72535040c3.text: Retired sailors later helped spread naval-style curry in Japan.

lxc_135ac331e1aee742.text: Whether people met curry through the navy, restaurants, or home cooking, the important point is adaptation: the dish changed to fit Japanese rice and daily life.

lxc_21a9835ed05d4aed.text: Curry became easier to cook when ready-made products improved.

lxc_00eb6a9d0486b98e.text: In 1923, food maker Minejiro Yamazaki produced the first curry powder made in Japan.

lxc_31c7bbc606af3918.text: In 1930, his company began selling the first curry powder for household use in Japan.

lxc_44b568de08e634d6.text: Curry roux later made the process even simpler.

lxc_91753d82ef5fe841.text: Roux blocks contain flour, oil or fat, spices, seasonings, and other ingredients.

lxc_577134f3cb56115c.text: A home cook can prepare meat and vegetables, add water, and melt the roux into the pot.

lxc_5c8253d955565cf8.text: The sauce becomes thick and gets a steady flavor.

lxc_11ceff4516d9a2ba.text: Curry roux is like a shortcut: it turns a large spice team into one easy block.

lxc_f123f6b4568bdb65.text: Japanese curry often feels different because several choices work together.

lxc_5af6371ff65a80cd.text: The sauce is usually thick, it is served with short-grain rice, and cooks can choose mild, medium, or hot roux.

lxc_bf5eca0f4bd66df5.text: Onions or fruit may add sweetness in some recipes.

lxc_f844c7e3fe196aff.text: Many people meet curry at home, in restaurants, or at school lunch, so its smell can bring back personal memories.

lxc_630ba968b11816b1.text: Curry began with ideas from outside Japan, but Japanese cooks and diners made it familiar.

lxc_ed0dec516fd67514.text: That is cultural adaptation: a food travels, changes, and becomes part of a new place.

lxc_535bb9cd4621b4e9.text: Curry is foreign and Japanese at the same time—and that is what makes its story fun.
